description_full: TE Connectivity plc, together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and sells connectivity and sensor solutions in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, the AsiaPacific, and the Americas. The company operates through two reportable segments, Transportation Solutions and Industrial Solutions. It provides antennas, application tooling, cable assemblies, connectors, electromagnetic compatibility/electromagnetic interference solutions, energy and power, fiber optics, heat shrink tubing, identification and labeling, medical components, passive components, relays and contactors, sensors, switches, terminals and splices, wires and cables, and wire protection and management solutions. The company also offers training and other services, including 3D printing for production, back shells prototyping, electrical installation training, HarnWare software, machine tooling service and repair, medical device design services, microfluidic devices, and sensor manufacturing services as well as conducts automotive webinars. It serves 5G and wireless equipment, aerospace, appliances, automation and control, automotive, autosport, commercial and industrial vehicles, connected home, data centers and artificial intelligence, defense and military, energy solutions, e-mobility, industrial machinery, intelligent buildings, IoT connectivity, medical technologies, oil and gas/marine, personal electronics and wearable technology, rail, sensor applications, space, and other industries. The company was formerly known as Tyco Electronics Ltd. and changed its name to TE Connectivity plc in March 2011. TE Connectivity plc was founded in 1941 and is based in Ballybrit, Ireland.

financial_summary: TE Connectivity plc is a large-cap technology business with a $57.3B market cap on $19.9B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +3.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 10% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 33%.

The business throws off $3.4B in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.39× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 32× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 13pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 21% below the high.

val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $304, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 35%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $210 to $444 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 18.1 vs 24.4, EV/EBITDA 12.9 vs 16.1 and P/FCF 16.8 vs 23.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 13% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 19 covering analysts target $258 on average, 29% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 10.5% by 7pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.07).
It runs a 33% gross margin and converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.39x.
ROE of 24% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.8x net debt to EBITDA ($1.7B of cash against $5.6B of debt), with interest covered 32.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.4% over 3 years, 5.9% over 5 years and 5.0% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 35% of profits supports about 6.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.4% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 5.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 100%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $8.2M sold).
It returns 4.8% a year to shareholders (3.3% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 18 consecutive years, raising it 6.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 90,000 employees, each generates about $221K of revenue, 0.6x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 4.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $38K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.2M (10x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
